# Lead-Time Recovery Plan: From 14 Weeks to 6–7, With Every Quality Gate Intact

Three functions — production, quality, and sales — have each been carrying their own pressure, and each sees a different part of this problem. None of them is wrong. The 14 weeks is not anyone's failure; it is the arithmetic sum of three groups each doing exactly what they were asked to do. This plan succeeds by giving all three a shared goal, shared facts, and shared protection — and by treating the warranty experience of two years ago not as a scar, but as the organization's most valuable asset: precise knowledge of what must never be rushed.

## 1. The Business Case

One in three deals lost on delivery speed is the financial engine of this plan. Illustrative figures below — the pod's first task, working quietly with finance and sales colleagues, is to rebuild them with actuals before any spending decision is taken.

| Element | Illustrative Estimate | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Quoted demand lost annually to lead time | ~$16M | $50M annual quoted pipeline × ~33% lost on delivery |
| Revenue recovered if half of those deals are won | ~$8M/yr | Parity on standard configurations + reliable promises on specials |
| Contribution margin recovered | ~$2.4–2.8M/yr | At 30–35% contribution |
| One-time investment | ~$2.0–3.5M | Module stock build ($1.5–2.5M working capital, partially offset by consignment), second-source qualification ($100–300k), operator training ($150–250k), digital traveler implementation ($200–400k), pod backfill (2–3 FTE-equivalents) |
| Recurring cost | ~$300–500k/yr | Carrying cost at 15–20% of module inventory; supplier capacity reservation fees |
| Payback | Under 12 months | Recovering even one deal in six covers the recurring costs several times over |

No executive is asked to approve this on placeholders. The structure is the commitment; the numbers are confirmed together, early, before money moves.

## 2. Where the 14 Weeks Actually Live

Before changing anything, the organization needs one shared fact base. Timestamp the last 20–30 orders end-to-end, separating touch time from queue time. This must be introduced with care: the audit maps the *process*, never the people, and that pledge is made explicitly and kept visibly. Blame thrives in opacity; it is very hard to blame a timestamp.

Expected decomposition, to be confirmed by the audit:

| Bucket | Typical Range | What to Look For |
|---|---|---|
| Order-to-release | 2–3 weeks | Quote clarifications, incomplete specs, engineering review queues |
| Long-lead purchased items | 4–6 weeks | Castings, drives, specialty components — often the true critical path |
| Production queue vs. build | 2–3 weeks | Units waiting days for cells that touch them for hours |
| Certification logistics | 2–3 weeks | Inspector availability, third-party witness scheduling, documentation assembled after the work instead of during it |
| Stacked buffers | 1–2 weeks | Each function quietly padding to protect itself; buffers compound |

In parallel, codify the warranty post-mortem — not to assign fault, which would only reopen old wounds, but to convert it into an explicit **"never again" list**: the specific shortcuts that caused the spike, written down as hard design constraints. This list is what allows Quality to shift from veto-by-delay to veto-by-design, a far more honorable and far less lonely role.

## 3. The Core Strategy — and Its Safety Net

The central question: *why does the certification clock start only when the order arrives?* If the product is even partially modular, the largest lever is **assemble-to-order**: build and fully certify standard modules to stock, in calm conditions, on your own schedule. When an order lands, only final assembly, final test, and final certification remain. The gates do not disappear — they happen before the customer's clock starts.

This lever, however, rests on one load-bearing assumption: that the certification regime permits it. The plan therefore gates the inventory spend on that answer, and carries a contingency for every outcome:

- **Path A — Full pre-certification permitted.** Proceed as designed; standard configurations reach 6–7 weeks.
- **Path B — Partial permission.** Witnessed batch inspection, periodic surveillance of stocked modules, or internal inspectors qualified as authorized witnesses. Most of the benefit survives; standards land at 7–8 weeks.
- **Path C — Not permitted.** The structural lever is shelved and revisited annually. The remaining levers — queue compression, supplier lead-time reduction, certification logistics, scheduling discipline — still deliver a realistic 8–9 weeks. The roadmap bends; it does not collapse.

The certification body is approached in weeks 2–6, early and respectfully, with a quality plan in hand rather than a request for concession. That relationship is an investment regardless of the answer. **Decision gate at week 8–10: no module inventory is built until the path is confirmed.** All Phase 1 quick wins proceed in parallel regardless — they are valuable under every path.

## 4. The Workstreams

**Process and flow.** Reduce batch sizes and changeover times in the constrained cells — queue time is batch-size-driven. Run engineering clarification and procurement kickoff concurrently with final design, not after it. Move spec verification to the quote stage, so incomplete orders are caught before they enter the system rather than discovered inside it.

**Inventory and suppliers.** Consignment or vendor-managed stock of the five to ten true long-lead items; framework agreements reserving supplier capacity; rolling forecasts shared with those suppliers — their lead time is partly your forecast silence. Pre-qualify second sources for the longest items, accepting a small volume premium as insurance.

**Scheduling.** Finite-capacity scheduling, or at minimum drum-buffer-rope around the constraint. A reserved fast lane for standard configurations; specials route around it. Quotes generated from the actual schedule, not from habit.

**Quality gates — accelerated, never thinned.** Inspection moves upstream: source inspection, first-article verification, operator in-process checks with proper gauging, so defects are caught where they are created — rework loops are lead time too. Documentation is generated as work happens. Certification witness slots are pre-booked on a rolling forecast, with standing windows negotiated with the third-party body. Every gate that exists today exists at the end; not one is removed, and the "never again" list is enforced by design.

**Configuration control for certified stock.** This is the quiet risk that must be managed from day one: an engineering change to a stocked, certified module can invalidate its certification. Rules: all certified stock serialized and traceable to design revision; any engineering change affecting a certified module requires joint Quality and certification review before release; affected stock is quarantined pending disposition (re-inspect, rework, or scrap); stocked modules sit under a design freeze with planned revision windows, safety-related changes excepted and handled by immediate effectivity with a stock purge protocol; certification validity of stock audited on a fixed cadence.

**Capacity and the transition.** Building modules to stock while working the current backlog must not starve committed orders — that would trade one reputation problem for another. Phase 0 includes a capacity study of the constraint cell against backlog plus the module build plan. The transition is absorbed by: a defined overtime or weekend window on the constraint (temporary, 3–6 months), subcontracting non-certified fabrication and machining to approved suppliers under source inspection, and gradual module coverage — four to six weeks of pilot-family coverage first, not full finished goods. The standing rule: module builds fill slack and added capacity only, never displacing a committed customer order.

**Commercial.** A tiered quoting architecture, validated against a demand Pareto in Phase 0:

| Quote Tier | Target Share | Target Lead Time (Month 12) |
|---|---|---|
| Standard configurations | 60–70% of quotes | 6–7 weeks |
| Configured variants | 20–25% | 8–9 weeks |
| Engineered specials | 10–15% | Honest 10–12, sold on milestone transparency |

Enterprise-weighted average quoted lead time falls from 14 to roughly 7.5–8 — and on the quotes that decide the win rate, it falls by more than half. A quote configurator ties lead time to configuration. Sales incentives gain modest weight on order cleanliness and forecast accuracy; incomplete orders are a hidden delay factory, and today sales bears no cost for them. Two further points: first, verify early what the competitor's "6 weeks" actually covers — quoted versus shipped, and whether it excludes specials; if the real bar is 8, then 7 wins, and the entire problem resizes. Second, matching 6 rather than beating it is sufficient if the promise is *kept* — reliability of the quoted date, milestone transparency, and an unimpeachable certification record become the differentiators.

## 5. What Each Lever Contributes

The Phase 1 target of 14 → 10–11 weeks is derived, not asserted:

| Lever | Mechanism | Expected Saving |
|---|---|---|
| Spec verification at quote; clean order entry | Eliminates clarification loops | 0.5–1.0 wk |
| Concurrent engineering/procurement kickoff | Removes sequential idle time | 0.5–1.0 wk |
| Pre-booked witness slots; documentation-during-work (interim: dedicated documentation coordinator) | Removes certification logistics tail | 1.0–1.5 wks |
| Batch-size reduction and changeover work on constraint | Shrinks queue time | 0.5–1.0 wk |
| Framework agreements on top long-lead items | Shortens true critical path on affected orders | 0.5–1.5 wks |

Savings are not fully additive — the critical path shifts as each lever lands — so the plan commits conservatively to 10–11. Digital travelers are deliberately *not*

[ORIGINAL USER REQUEST]
An industrial equipment maker quotes 14-week lead times while its fastest competitor quotes 6, and sales reports losing one in three deals on delivery speed alone. The product requires certified quality inspections at multiple stages, and the last attempt to compress the schedule caused a spike in warranty claims that took two years to live down. Production, quality, and sales each blame the others' processes.

Develop an operations improvement plan that substantially reduces quoted lead time without compromising certified quality standards. Identify where time is actually lost, which process, inventory, scheduling, or supplier changes to make, how to protect quality gates, and how to align the three feuding functions around the plan.
[END ORIGINAL REQUEST]

[PREVIOUS AGENT OUTPUT]
# Lead-Time Compression: A Working Draft

Before the plan itself, one observation that keeps surfacing: the last compression attempt failed, and the instinct now is to treat "faster" and "certified" as opponents. But it's worth asking whether they actually were opponents last time — or whether someone compressed the *inspections* when the real slack was always in the *waiting*. Those are very different problems, and only one of them should scare you.

## Step One: Find Out Where the 14 Weeks Actually Live

It would be surprising if even half of the 14 weeks were touch time. In equipment businesses like this, the number usually decomposes something like this — offered as hypotheses to test, not conclusions:

- **Order-to-release:** quote clarifications, incomplete specs, engineering review queues — often 2–3 weeks before work formally "starts"
- **Long-lead purchased items:** castings, drives, specialty components — frequently the true critical path at 4–6 weeks
- **Production queue vs. build:** a unit may wait two weeks for a cell that touches it for four days
- **Certification logistics:** waiting for inspector availability, third-party witness scheduling, and documentation assembled *after* the work rather than *during* it — easily 2–3 weeks
- **Padding:** each function quietly adds buffer to protect itself, and buffers stack

The diagnostic is cheap and fast: timestamp the last 20–30 orders end-to-end, and separate touch time from queue time. Alongside it, a proper post-mortem of the warranty spike — not to assign blame, but to codify exactly what was skipped or rushed. That list becomes design constraints later. More on that below.

## The Strategic Reframe: Move the Decoupling Point

Here's the question worth sitting with: *why does the certification clock start only after the order arrives?*

If the product is even partially modular, the biggest single lever is shifting from make-to-order to **assemble-to-order**. Build and *fully certify* standard modules and subassemblies to stock, on your own schedule, with inspections done in calm conditions. When an order lands, the remaining work is final assembly, final test, and final certification — a fraction of today's critical path. The in-process quality gates don't disappear; they happen *before* the customer's clock starts ticking.

This only works, of course, if the product is modularized around a stable option set — which suggests a parallel conversation with engineering about what percentage of demand could be served by, say, ten pre-certified configurations. Eighty percent is a common answer, and eighty percent is enough to change the game.

## The Specific Moves

**Process and flow**
- Reduce batch sizes and attack changeover times in the constrained cells — queue time is usually batch-size-driven
- Run engineering clarification and procurement kickoff *concurrently* with final design, not sequentially after it
- Move order review upstream: specs completed and verified at quote stage, not discovered missing at order entry

**Inventory and suppliers**
- Strategic stock — ideally consignment or vendor-managed — of the five to ten true long-lead items, with framework agreements reserving supplier capacity
- Share rolling forecasts with those suppliers; their lead time is partly your forecast silence
- Pre-qualify second sources for the longest items, even at a small volume premium

**Scheduling**
- Replace padded, infinite-loaded schedules with finite-capacity scheduling — or at minimum a drum-buffer-rope discipline around the constraint
- Reserve a slice of capacity as a **fast lane** for standard configurations; specials route around it
- Quote from the actual schedule, not from historical habit

**Quality gates — faster, never weaker**
This is where the plan lives or dies, given the history. The distinction to hold firmly: *accelerate the gates; never thin them.*

- Move inspection upstream — source inspection, first-article verification, operator in-process checks with proper gauging — so defects are caught where they're created. Rework loops are lead time too.
- Digital quality travelers: documentation generated as work happens, not compiled afterward. The paperwork tail is often a hidden week.
- Pre-book certification witness slots on a rolling forecast; negotiate standing windows with the third-party body rather than scheduling ad hoc. In some regimes, it's also worth exploring whether internal inspectors can be qualified as authorized witnesses under surveillance — that question alone can be worth a week.
- The warranty post-mortem becomes an explicit **"never again" list** — the specific shortcuts that caused the spike, codified as hard constraints. This converts Quality's role from veto-by-delay to veto-by-design, which is a much healthier job for them and a much safer one for you.

**The sales side — quietly important**
- Tiered quoting: standard configurations at a genuinely competitive number (6–7 weeks is plausible within two quarters), configured variants slightly longer, engineered specials quoted honestly with milestone transparency as the selling point
- A quote configurator so lead time reflects the configuration, not a flat 14 that over-promises on simple orders and under-serves the urgent ones
- Some modest incentive weight on order cleanliness and forecast accuracy — incomplete orders are a hidden delay factory, and sales currently bears no cost for them

It may also be worth quietly verifying what the competitor's "6 weeks" actually covers — quoted versus shipped, and whether it excludes specials. Sometimes the gap is smaller than the legend.

## Aligning Three Feuding Functions

A thought: perhaps production, quality, and sales aren't broken — perhaps each is rationally optimizing what it's measured on, and the 14 weeks is the arithmetic sum of three local optima. Blame thrives in opacity; it's hard to blame a timestamp.

So rather than a steering committee or a program office — structures that tend to reproduce the hierarchy that created the problem — consider a small **cross-functional pod**: one credible person from each function, chosen for expertise rather than rank, with a clear charter, a shared dashboard showing every order's timestamps, and one shared metric:

> **Quoted lead time at 100% gate pass rate** — with warranty rate and first-pass yield as inviolable guardrails.

Rotating facilitation, weekly short-cycle reviews, and explicit protection from interference. The pod owns the pilot; it doesn't ask permission for each experiment within the guardrails.

## Phasing and Guardrails

- **Weeks 0–4:** Timestamp audit, value stream map, warranty post-mortem codified, long-lead items and top configurations identified
- **Weeks 4–12:** Quick wins — clean order entry, pre-booked witness slots, digital travelers, finite scheduling, fast-lane pilot on one configuration family. Expect 14 → 10–11 here.
- **Months 3–6:** Structural — pre-certified module stock, supplier agreements, capacity reservation. The pilot family should be quoting 7–8 by now.
- **Months 6–12:** Scale across lines; standard configurations quoting 6–7.

Guardrails throughout: first-pass yield, gate pass rates, and warranty claims reviewed monthly. Expansion to the next product family only after the pilot holds quality metrics across a meaningful number of orders. If a leading indicator flickers, the plan slows — that rule, stated in advance, is what buys Quality's trust and what distinguishes this attempt from the last one.

## Questions Left Open

A few things this draft can't answer from the outside: How modular is the product really? What does the certification regime permit regarding witness arrangements? Which single purchased item has the longest lead, and would its supplier hold stock? And — perhaps most telling — what exactly did the post-mortem on the warranty spike find, assuming one was ever written down?

If any of those answers are available, the plan sharpens considerably. Happy to push further into whichever thread seems most alive.
[END PREVIOUS OUTPUT]

[QUALITY FEEDBACK FROM Critic]
# Critique of Previous Output

## What Works

The output covers all five requested elements, and its central insight — shifting to assemble-to-order with pre-certified modules so inspection happens before the customer's clock starts — is genuinely strong. The "accelerate the gates, never thin them" principle, the touch-time vs. queue-time distinction, and the warranty post-mortem-as-design-constraints move are all expert-level. The alignment section correctly diagnoses the feud as three local optima rather than three broken teams.

## Specific Weaknesses

**1. No business case.** This is the largest gap. The plan proposes strategic inventory, consignment stock, pre-certified module builds, second-source qualification, and a dedicated pod — none of it costed. Meanwhile, the prompt hands the author the financial hook (losing one in three deals on delivery speed) and the output never converts that into a revenue-recovery estimate. No executive approves this plan without: working capital impact of module inventory, cost of reserved supplier capacity, and expected payback from recovered win rate. The persona is supposed to be data-driven; this output is qualitatively argued throughout.

**2. # Lead-Time Compression: A Working Draft

Before the plan itself, one observation that keeps surfacing: the last compression attempt failed, and the instinct now is to treat "faster" and "certified" as opponents. But it's worth asking whether they actually were opponents last time — or whether someone compressed the *inspections* when the real slack was always in the *waiting*. Those are very different problems, and only one of them should scare you.

## Step One: Find Out Where the 14 Weeks Actually Live

It would be surprising if even half of the 14 weeks were touch time. In equipment businesses like this, the number usually decomposes something like this — offered as hypotheses to test, not conclusions:

- **Order-to-release:** quote clarifications, incomplete specs, engineering review queues — often 2–3 weeks before work formally "starts"
- **Long-lead purchased items:** castings, drives, specialty components — frequently the true critical path at 4–6 weeks
- **Production queue vs. build:** a unit may wait two weeks for a cell that touches it for four days
- **Certification logistics:** waiting for inspector availability, third-party witness scheduling, and documentation assembled *after* the work rather than *during* it — easily 2–3 weeks
- **Padding:** each function quietly adds buffer to protect itself, and buffers stack

The diagnostic is cheap and fast: timestamp the last 20–30 orders end-to-end, and separate touch time from queue time. Alongside it, a proper post-mortem of the warranty spike — not to assign blame, but to codify exactly what was skipped or rushed. That list becomes design constraints later. More on that below.

## The Strategic Reframe: Move the Decoupling Point

Here's the question worth sitting with: *why does the certification clock start only after the order arrives?*

If the product is even partially modular, the biggest single lever is shifting from make-to-order to **assemble-to-order**. Build and *fully certify* standard modules and subassemblies to stock, on your own schedule, with inspections done in calm conditions. When an order lands, the remaining work is final assembly, final test, and final certification — a fraction of today's critical path. The in-process quality gates don't disappear; they happen *before* the customer's clock starts ticking.

This only works, of course, if the product is modularized around a stable option set — which suggests a parallel conversation with engineering about what percentage of demand could be served by, say, ten pre-certified configurations. Eighty percent is a common answer, and eighty percent is enough to change the game.

## The Specific Moves

**Process and flow**
- Reduce batch sizes and attack changeover times in the constrained cells — queue time is usually batch-size-driven
- Run engineering clarification and procurement kickoff *concurrently* with final design, not sequentially after it
- Move order review upstream: specs completed and verified at quote stage, not discovered missing at order entry

**Inventory and suppliers**
- Strategic stock — ideally consignment or vendor-managed — of the five to ten true long-lead items, with framework agreements reserving supplier capacity
- Share rolling forecasts with those suppliers; their lead time is partly your forecast silence
- Pre-qualify second sources for the longest items, even at a small volume premium

**Scheduling**
- Replace padded, infinite-loaded schedules with finite-capacity scheduling — or at minimum a drum-buffer-rope discipline around the constraint
- Reserve a slice of capacity as a **fast lane** for standard configurations; specials route around it
- Quote from the actual schedule, not from historical habit

**Quality gates — faster, never weaker**
This is where the plan lives or dies, given the history. The distinction to hold firmly: *accelerate the gates; never thin them.*

- Digital quality travelers: documentation generated as work happens, not compiled afterward. The paperwork tail is often a hidden week.
- Pre-book certification witness slots on a rolling forecast; negotiate standing windows with the third-party body rather than scheduling ad hoc. - The warranty post-mortem becomes an explicit **"never again" list** — the specific shortcuts that caused the spike, codified as hard constraints. This converts Quality's role from veto-by-delay to veto-by-design, which is a much healthier job for them and a much safer one for you.

**The sales side — quietly important**
- Tiered quoting: standard configurations at a genuinely competitive number (6–7 weeks is plausible within two quarters), configured variants slightly longer, engineered specials quoted honestly with milestone transparency as the selling point

## Aligning Three Feuding Functions

A thought: perhaps production, quality, and sales aren't broken — perhaps each is rationally optimizing what it's measured on, and the 14 weeks is the arithmetic sum of three local optima. Blame thrives in opacity; it's hard to blame a timestamp.

A few things this draft can't answer from the outside: How modular is the product really? What does the certification regime permit regarding witness arrangements? Which single purchased item has the longest lead, and would its supplier hold stock? # Lead-Time Recovery Plan: From 14 Weeks to 6–7, With Every Quality Gate Intact

Three functions — production, quality, and sales — have each been carrying their own pressure, and each sees a different part of this problem. None of them is wrong. The 14 weeks is not anyone's failure; it is the arithmetic sum of three groups each doing exactly what they were asked to do. This plan succeeds by giving all three a shared goal, shared facts, and shared protection — and by treating the warranty experience of two years ago not as a scar, but as the organization's most valuable asset: precise knowledge of what must never be rushed.

## 1. The Business Case

One in three deals lost on delivery speed is the financial engine of this plan. Illustrative figures below — the pod's first task, working quietly with finance and sales colleagues, is to rebuild them with actuals before any spending decision is taken.

| Element | Illustrative Estimate | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Quoted demand lost annually to lead time | ~$16M | $50M annual quoted pipeline × ~33% lost on delivery |
| Revenue recovered if half of those deals are won | ~$8M/yr | Parity on standard configurations + reliable promises on specials |
| Contribution margin recovered | ~$2.4–2.8M/yr | At 30–35% contribution |
| One-time investment | ~$2.0–3.5M | Module stock build ($1.5–2.5M working capital, partially offset by consignment), second-source qualification ($100–300k), operator training ($150–250k), digital traveler implementation ($200–400k), pod backfill (2–3 FTE-equivalents) |
| Recurring cost | ~$300–500k/yr | Carrying cost at 15–20% of module inventory; supplier capacity reservation fees |
| Payback | Under 12 months | Recovering even one deal in six covers the recurring costs several times over |

No executive is asked to approve this on placeholders. The structure is the commitment; the numbers are confirmed together, early, before money moves.

## 2. Where the 14 Weeks Actually Live

Before changing anything, the organization needs one shared fact base. Timestamp the last 20–30 orders end-to-end, separating touch time from queue time. This must be introduced with care: the audit maps the *process*, never the people, and that pledge is made explicitly and kept visibly. Blame thrives in opacity; it is very hard to blame a timestamp.

Expected decomposition, to be confirmed by the audit:

| Bucket | Typical Range | What to Look For |
|---|---|---|
| Order-to-release | 2–3 weeks | Quote clarifications, incomplete specs, engineering review queues |
| Long-lead purchased items | 4–6 weeks | Castings, drives, specialty components — often the true critical path |
| Production queue vs. build | 2–3 weeks | Units waiting days for cells that touch them for hours |
| Certification logistics | 2–3 weeks | Inspector availability, third-party witness scheduling, documentation assembled after the work instead of during it |
| Stacked buffers | 1–2 weeks | Each function quietly padding to protect itself; buffers compound |

In parallel, codify the warranty post-mortem — not to assign fault, which would only reopen old wounds, but to convert it into an explicit **"never again" list**: the specific shortcuts that caused the spike, written down as hard design constraints. This list is what allows Quality to shift from veto-by-delay to veto-by-design, a far more honorable and far less lonely role.

## 3. The Core Strategy — and Its Safety Net

The central question: *why does the certification clock start only when the order arrives?* If the product is even partially modular, the largest lever is **assemble-to-order**: build and fully certify standard modules to stock, in calm conditions, on your own schedule. When an order lands, only final assembly, final test, and final certification remain. The gates do not disappear — they happen before the customer's clock starts.

This lever, however, rests on one load-bearing assumption: that the certification regime permits it. The plan therefore gates the inventory spend on that answer, and carries a contingency for every outcome:

- **Path A — Full pre-certification permitted.** Proceed as designed; standard configurations reach 6–7 weeks.
- **Path B — Partial permission.** Witnessed batch inspection, periodic surveillance of stocked modules, or internal inspectors qualified as authorized witnesses. Most of the benefit survives; standards land at 7–8 weeks.
- **Path C — Not permitted.** The structural lever is shelved and revisited annually. The remaining levers — queue compression, supplier lead-time reduction, certification logistics, scheduling discipline — still deliver a realistic 8–9 weeks. The roadmap bends; it does not collapse.

The certification body is approached in weeks 2–6, early and respectfully, with a quality plan in hand rather than a request for concession. That relationship is an investment regardless of the answer. **Decision gate at week 8–10: no module inventory is built until the path is confirmed.** All Phase 1 quick wins proceed in parallel regardless — they are valuable under every path.

## 4. The Workstreams

**Process and flow.** Reduce batch sizes and changeover times in the constrained cells — queue time is batch-size-driven. Run engineering clarification and procurement kickoff concurrently with final design, not after it. Move spec verification to the quote stage, so incomplete orders are caught before they enter the system rather than discovered inside it.

**Inventory and suppliers.** Consignment or vendor-managed stock of the five to ten true long-lead items; framework agreements reserving supplier capacity; rolling forecasts shared with those suppliers — their lead time is partly your forecast silence. Pre-qualify second sources for the longest items, accepting a small volume premium as insurance.

**Scheduling.** Finite-capacity scheduling, or at minimum drum-buffer-rope around the constraint. A reserved fast lane for standard configurations; specials route around it. Quotes generated from the actual schedule, not from habit.

**Quality gates — accelerated, never thinned.** Inspection moves upstream: source inspection, first-article verification, operator in-process checks with proper gauging, so defects are caught where they are created — rework loops are lead time too. Documentation is generated as work happens. Certification witness slots are pre-booked on a rolling forecast, with standing windows negotiated with the third-party body. Every gate that exists today exists at the end; not one is removed, and the "never again" list is enforced by design.

**Configuration control for certified stock.** This is the quiet risk that must be managed from day one: an engineering change to a stocked, certified module can invalidate its certification. Rules: all certified stock serialized and traceable to design revision; any engineering change affecting a certified module requires joint Quality and certification review before release; affected stock is quarantined pending disposition (re-inspect, rework, or scrap); stocked modules sit under a design freeze with planned revision windows, safety-related changes excepted and handled by immediate effectivity with a stock purge protocol; certification validity of stock audited on a fixed cadence.

**Capacity and the transition.** Building modules to stock while working the current backlog must not starve committed orders — that would trade one reputation problem for another. Phase 0 includes a capacity study of the constraint cell against backlog plus the module build plan. The transition is absorbed by: a defined overtime or weekend window on the constraint (temporary, 3–6 months), subcontracting non-certified fabrication and machining to approved suppliers under source inspection, and gradual module coverage — four to six weeks of pilot-family coverage first, not full finished goods. The standing rule: module builds fill slack and added capacity only, never displacing a committed customer order.

**Commercial.** A tiered quoting architecture, validated against a demand Pareto in Phase 0:

| Quote Tier | Target Share | Target Lead Time (Month 12) |
|---|---|---|
| Standard configurations | 60–70% of quotes | 6–7 weeks |
| Configured variants | 20–25% | 8–9 weeks |
| Engineered specials | 10–15% | Honest 10–12, sold on milestone transparency |

Enterprise-weighted average quoted lead time falls from 14 to roughly 7.5–8 — and on the quotes that decide the win rate, it falls by more than half. A quote configurator ties lead time to configuration. Sales incentives gain modest weight on order cleanliness and forecast accuracy; incomplete orders are a hidden delay factory, and today sales bears no cost for them. Two further points: first, verify early what the competitor's "6 weeks" actually covers — quoted versus shipped, and whether it excludes specials; if the real bar is 8, then 7 wins, and the entire problem resizes. Second, matching 6 rather than beating it is sufficient if the promise is *kept* — reliability of the quoted date, milestone transparency, and an unimpeachable certification record become the differentiators.

## 5. What Each Lever Contributes

The Phase 1 target of 14 → 10–11 weeks is derived, not asserted:

| Lever | Mechanism | Expected Saving |
|---|---|---|
| Spec verification at quote; clean order entry | Eliminates clarification loops | 0.5–1.0 wk |
| Concurrent engineering/procurement kickoff | Removes sequential idle time | 0.5–1.0 wk |
| Pre-booked witness slots; documentation-during-work (interim: dedicated documentation coordinator) | Removes certification logistics tail | 1.0–1.5 wks |
| Batch-size reduction and changeover work on constraint | Shrinks queue time | 0.5–1.0 wk |
| Framework agreements on top long-lead items | Shortens true critical path on affected orders | 0.5–1.5 wks |

Savings are not fully additive — the critical path shifts as each lever lands — so the plan commits conservatively to 10–11. Digital travelers are deliberately *not*
